title: Jeremiah 39:11–18
context: Jeremiah 39:11–18 has two parts. In 39:11–14 the narrator reports that Nebuchadnezzar commanded Nebuzaradan to take care of Jeremiah, and that Nebuzaradan and the Babylonian officers took Jeremiah out of the court of the guard and committed him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, so that he lived among the people. The names Nebushazban, Rabsaris, and Rabmag in 39:13 again raise questions of names and titles that are not settled here. Gedaliah’s father Ahikam had protected Jeremiah earlier (26:24, “the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah”). The account of Jeremiah’s release here and in 38:28 should be read alongside 40:1, where Nebuzaradan lets Jeremiah go at Ramah after he had been taken in chains among the captives; readers suggest a release in stages or two distinct traditions of the event, and these notes leave the relation unresolved. In 39:15–18 the narrator looks back to a word the LORD gave Jeremiah while he was still shut up in the court of the guard, for Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, the court official who had rescued Jeremiah from the dungeon (38:7–13). The LORD promises that though the city will fall, Ebedmelech will not be given into the hands of those he fears, “because you have put your trust in me” (39:18; compare 17:7; 21:9; 45:5). Both traditions read this promise as largely shared ground: the LORD honors those who trust him and remembers the kindness shown to his servant, and the notes do not draw a new contrast from it.

verses.text: Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon commanded Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard concerning Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuchadnezzar commanded Nebuzaradan concerning Jeremiah. Arminian readers note the surprising turn in which the conquering king gives orders to protect the prophet whom Judah’s own leaders had imprisoned, and they see God’s care for his servant working through unexpected means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and read the king’s command within God’s providence over the nations and his faithfulness to his prophet. They observe that the text does not say how Nebuchadnezzar knew of Jeremiah, and they do not speculate beyond what it records.

verses.text: “Take him and take care of him. Do him no harm; but do to him even as he tells you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuchadnezzar said, “Take him and take care of him. Do him no harm; but do to him even as he tells you.” Arminian readers note the generosity of the order, which gives Jeremiah a say in his own treatment, and they see in it the LORD’s protection of the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the command places Jeremiah’s welfare under the protection of the empire that had destroyed the city. They read it as one of several ways the book shows the LORD keeping his promise to deliver Jeremiah from those who sought his life (compare 1:8).

verses.text: So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban, Rabsaris, and Nergal Sharezer, Rabmag, and all the chief officers of the king of Babylon
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan, Nebushazban the Rabsaris, Nergal Sharezer the Rabmag, and the chief officers of Babylon acted on the order. Arminian readers note that the names and titles again raise questions of identification, and they hold them loosely while noting the high rank of those involved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these lists of Babylonian officials are difficult to reconcile in detail with 39:3, and they do not harmonize them. They read the verse as emphasizing that Jeremiah’s release was carried out by the highest authorities present.

verses.text: sent and took Jeremiah out of the court of the guard, and committed him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, that he should bring him home. So he lived among the people.
verses.arminianNotes: They took Jeremiah out of the court of the guard and committed him to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, so that he lived among the people. Arminian readers note the link with 38:28 and the question of how this relates to 40:1, where Jeremiah is released at Ramah, and they leave it unresolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same question and observe that interpreters propose a release in stages or two accounts of the event, without settling it. They also note that Gedaliah’s father Ahikam had protected Jeremiah before (26:24), named here without harmonizing.

verses.text: Now the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard. Arminian readers note that the narrator steps back in time to report this word, and they see in it the LORD’s attention to one faithful individual even as the city’s fate is sealed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the flashback places the promise to Ebedmelech before the city’s fall, so that its fulfillment can be seen in what follows. They read the verse as showing that God’s word governs both the judgment of the city and the rescue of his servant.

verses.text: “Go, and speak to Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will bring my words on this city for evil, and not for good; and they will be accomplished before you in that day.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to speak to Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying that the LORD will bring his words on the city for evil and not for good. Arminian readers note the link with 38:7–13, where Ebedmelech rescued Jeremiah, and they see God noticing a foreigner’s courage and compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link and observe that Ebedmelech is described in 38:7 as “Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a eunuch, who was in the king’s house”. They read the word to him as showing that the LORD’s care extends to a foreigner who acted rightly toward his prophet.

verses.text: But I will deliver you in that day,” says the LORD; “and you will not be given into the hand of the men of whom you are afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “But I will deliver you in that day,” and that Ebedmelech will not be given into the hand of the men he fears. Arminian readers note the personal promise of deliverance amid national disaster, and they see in it God’s faithfulness to those who trust him in dangerous times.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same promise and observe that the men he feared may be the Babylonians or the Judean officials he had opposed, since the text does not say. They read the verse as shared ground on God’s protection of his servants, without drawing a new contrast from it.

verses.text: For I will surely save you. You won’t fall by the sword, but you will escape with your life, because you have put your trust in me,” says the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “For I will surely save you”, because “you have put your trust in me”. Arminian readers note that the promise is linked to Ebedmelech’s trust, and they compare 17:7, “Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD”, named here without harmonizing, as shared ground on trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link and compare the promise to Baruch, “I will let you escape with your life wherever you go” (45:5), and 21:9. They read Ebedmelech’s trust as the fruit of God’s grace and his deliverance as God’s gift, which both traditions treat as largely shared ground.
